title: Slope gets its name, and the bridges of Konigsberg
summary: Turn last season's informal per into slope, build the law of a line out of your own tally and walk it on a chalk grid, then chalk the seven bridges of Konigsberg on the driveway and hunt for whatever it is that decides which drawings can be walked in one stroke.
materials: jumbo sidewalk chalk and a driveway or path
the desert wall map: poster board, markers and flag pins

problems.prompt: Five dawn walks measured 1.4 km, 2.1 km, 0.9 km, 1.8 km and 2.3 km. Round each one to the nearest whole kilometre, then add the rounded numbers. What total do you get?
explanation: Round each walk on its own: 1, 2, 1, 2, 2.
Add those five rounded numbers.
The true total is 8.5, so the estimate came out light, even though no single walk moved by as much as half a kilometre.
problems.useAgain: when you want a quick total and the exact decimals would slow you down more than they help.
hints: Round every walk on its own before you add anything at all.
Anything below the halfway mark rounds down, anything above it rounds up.
problems.socraticHint: Did more of the five round up or down, and does that tell you which side of the truth your estimate is sitting on?

variant.prompt: Round 1.6 km, 0.3 km and 2.8 km to the nearest whole kilometre, then add the rounded numbers.

problems.prompt: One kind of number box in C++ holds whole numbers up to 2,147,483,647 and no further. Round that number to the nearest million.
explanation: Split it into whole millions and a leftover: 2,147 millions, with 483,647 left over.
Half a million is 500,000, and the leftover is smaller than that.
So the number is nearer to 2,147 millions than to 2,148 millions, and the count of millions stays where it is.
problems.useAgain: when rounding a big number and you need to know which of the two neighbours it sits nearer to.
hints: Split it into whole millions and whatever is left over.
Compare that leftover with half a million and ignore everything else.
problems.socraticHint: Would your answer change if the leftover had begun with a five instead?

variant.prompt: Round 2,147,483,647 to the nearest hundred thousand.

problems.prompt: A chalk grid is drawn 9 squares across, and each square is 40 cm on a side. About how far across is the whole grid?
explanation: Nine squares of 40 cm is nine lots of 40, which is 360 cm.
A metre is 100 cm, so 360 cm is 3.6 metres.
Of the four sizes offered, 4 metres is the one 3.6 sits closest to.
problems.useAgain: when a question says about and you only need to land near the right size.
hints: Work it out in centimetres first and turn the answer into metres at the very end.
Nine lots of 40 is easier as ten lots of 40 with one lot taken back off.
problems.socraticHint: If each square were half as wide, would the grid still be about this size?

variant.prompt: A chalk grid is 12 squares across and each square is 25 cm on a side. About how far across is it?

problems.prompt: True or false: a path that rises 3 metres for every 2 metres forward is steeper than a path that rises 5 metres for every 4 metres forward.
explanation: Steepness is the rise for one single step forward, so bring both paths down to one metre forward.
Rising 3 for every 2 forward is rising 1.5 for every 1.
Rising 5 for every 4 forward is rising 1.25 for every 1, which is less, so the first path really is the steeper one.
problems.useAgain: when two pers are written with different bottoms and you need them on the same footing before comparing.
hints: Bigger numbers on both sides do not mean steeper. Compare the rise for the same step forward.
Turn each pair into how much it rises for one metre forward.
problems.socraticHint: If a path rose a hundred metres for every hundred metres forward, would those big numbers make it steep?

variant.prompt: True or false: a path that rises 4 metres for every 6 metres forward is steeper than a path that rises 3 metres for every 4 metres forward.

problem.prompt: On graph paper mark the corner 0 across, 0 up and the corner 12 across, 8 up, then rule one straight line between them. Not counting the corner you started on, how many grid corners does that line pass exactly through?
explanation: The line climbs 8 up for 12 across, and that per tidies to 2 up for every 3 across.
So from any corner the line touches, the next one is 3 along and 2 up. Nothing in between counts, because a third of a square is not a corner.
Start at 0 and 0 and take that step again and again. It lands on 3 and 2, then on 6 and 4, then on 9 and 6, and last of all on the far end.
Counting the far end and not the start, the line passes exactly through 4 corners.
Then rule it and walk a pencil point along it. The corners it misses are the interesting part.
problem.useAgain: when a straight line crosses a grid and you want the places it lands on a corner rather than inside a square.
hints: Tidy the line's per down to lowest terms before you count anything. That tidied fraction is the size of one step.
From a corner the line touches, how far along and how far up is the very next corner it touches?
problem.socraticHint: Would the count change if the line ran to 6 across and 9 up instead, and what is different about those two numbers?

variant.prompt: The same job on a line ruled from the corner 0 across, 0 up to the corner 15 across, 9 up. Not counting the corner you started on, how many grid corners does it pass exactly through?

steps.title: The desert map goes on the wall
steps.body:
Fourth map, last terrain. The poster board goes up today and stays up all summer.

Twelve waypoints across it, one for each quest week. Some of them get a sun drawn beside them, one sun for each crossing morning, and those are the only weekend mornings this whole season carries anything at all. The plan asks for three. A grown-up settles which three dates today, with you at the map, and you draw a sun on each one, rather than leaving them to be found later in a hurry.

Two far stars sit out past the edge of the map, with their real dates written beside them once a grown-up has looked them up: the first real contest sitting in December, and AMC 8 in January. You steer by them and you do not reach either one this summer, because steering is what stars are for. Neither of them happens inside this season and neither of them is the point of it.

Two things are different this year, and both get said out loud rather than sneaked past you. A timer, which until now belonged only to debate, runs on those crossing mornings. And weekends, which have never carried anything, carry those mornings. Those are the two that touch these first weeks, and every other piece of work this summer is untimed, including every peak in this lane. If anything else changes later in the season, you hear about it the same way, out loud and before it happens.

One rule the map does not bend: it shows dates, never counts. No days remaining, nothing that shrinks as the summer goes. If you catch anybody writing a countdown on it, rub it out.

steps.title: Slope: the per, and the law of a line

problems.prompt: At the oasis market, a caravan train counts its animals: only camels, with 4 legs each, and ostriches, with 2 legs each. The count comes to 15 heads and 46 legs altogether. How many camels are in the caravan?
explanation: Two facts, two unknowns is the idea here: one equation alone cannot separate camels from ostriches, since fifteen heads could be almost any mix.
The leg count is the second fact, since camels have 4 legs and ostriches have 2.
Swap the head fact into the leg fact: with ostriches equal to 15 minus the camels, 4 camels plus 2 times that gives 46.
That tidies to 2 times the camels plus 30 equals 46, so the camels are 8, leaving 7 ostriches.
Check: 4 times 8 plus 2 times 7 is 32 plus 14, which is 46.
problems.useAgain: when a question hands you two different kinds of thing and only their combined head count and combined total.
hints: One count alone cannot separate two kinds of thing. Find the second fact before you try anything.
Trade one fact into the other: write one animal as 15 minus the other, then use that in the leg total.
problems.socraticHint: If every animal in the caravan had the same number of legs, could the head count and the leg count ever disagree with each other?

variant.prompt: A second caravan train counts 20 heads and 64 legs, again only camels and ostriches. How many camels are in that caravan?

problems.prompt: On the chalk grid a line passes through the corner 1 across, 7 up and through the corner 5 across, 1 up. What is its slope?
explanation: Slope is a per: how much the up amount changes for every single step across. That per is what this whole idea is called.
Walking from the first corner to the second, the up amount goes from 7 to 1, a change of minus 6.
The across amount goes from 1 to 5, a change of 4.
Slope is the up change shared among the across change, then tidied.
The minus sign is the line falling as you walk right. It belongs in the answer.
problems.useAgain: when you have two corners a line passes through and you want the line's per.
hints: Subtract in the same direction for both amounts, up first and then across, and keep whatever sign comes out.
A slope is one change divided by the other, so tidy the fraction once you have it.
problems.socraticHint: Walking this line from left to right, are you going uphill or downhill, and what should that do to the sign?

variant.prompt: On the chalk grid a line passes through the corner 0 across, 8 up and through the corner 6 across, 2 up. What is its slope?

problems.prompt: Suppose a stand costs 6 dollars for the table plus 2 dollars of materials for every bracelet made. What does making 10 bracelets cost altogether?
explanation: A line is a starting amount plus the same step over and over. Know both and you know the whole line.
The starting amount is the 6 dollar table, paid once whether you make ten bracelets or none.
The step is 2 dollars a bracelet, so ten bracelets take ten steps, which is 20 dollars.
Add the start to the steps: 6 dollars plus 20 dollars.
Written as a law, the cost is 2 times the count of bracelets, plus 6.
problems.useAgain: when something starts at one amount and then changes by the same amount every single time.
hints: Two different kinds of cost are hiding in here. One happens once, the other happens per bracelet.
Work out the materials for ten bracelets first, then add the thing that only ever happens once.
problems.socraticHint: What would the day cost if no bracelets were made at all, and where does that amount live in the law?

variant.prompt: Suppose the table costs 9 dollars and materials are 1.50 dollars a bracelet. What does making 12 bracelets cost altogether?

problems.prompt:
Marcus found the slope of the line through the corner 2 across, 3 up and the corner 6 across, 11 up, like this:
Line 1: The across amount changes from 2 to 6, a change of 4.
Line 2: The up amount changes from 3 to 11, a change of 8.
Line 3: Slope is the across change shared among the up change, so slope is 4 over 8.
Line 4: Tidied, that slope is 1/2.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 3 is wrong: slope is the up change shared among the across change, not the other way round.
Lines 1 and 2 both correctly find the two changes: across changes by 4, and up changes by 8.
Line 4 correctly tidies the fraction Line 3 handed it, 4 over 8 to 1 over 2, but that fraction was already upside down.
The true slope is 8 shared among 4, which is 2. Flipping which change goes on top flips the whole answer.
problems.useAgain: when you calculate a slope and want to check you divided the two changes in the right order and kept their signs.
hints: Every line's arithmetic is done correctly. Look at which two numbers get divided, and in which order.
Check the direction of each change too, not just its size. Going down still counts as a change.
problems.socraticHint: If you walked this line from left to right, would you be walking uphill or downhill, and does the answer agree?

variant.prompt:
Priya found the slope of the line through the corner 1 across, 10 up and the corner 5 across, 2 up, like this:
Line 1: The across amount changes from 1 to 5, a change of 4.
Line 2: The up amount changes from 10 to 2, a change of 8.
Line 3: Slope is the up change shared among the across change, so slope is 8 over 4.
Line 4: Tidied, that slope is 2.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Suppose two walkers keep steady paces. Ana's distance from the gate after t minutes is d = 70t + 200. Ben's is d = 90t. Which sentence is true?
options: Ben starts ahead of Ana and walks faster
Ana starts ahead of Ben and walks faster
They start level and walk at the same pace
Ana starts ahead of Ben and Ben walks faster
explanation: The part with no t says where somebody is at the start. Ana is 200 m along, Ben is at the gate.
The number multiplying t is the per: metres for every minute.
Ana covers 70 metres a minute and Ben covers 90. So Ben is faster, even though Ana starts out in front.
problems.useAgain: when a law is handed to you already written and you need to say what its two parts mean in the real world.
hints: Read the two parts of each law separately: the part with t and the part without it.
Put t as nothing in both laws and see where each walker is standing.
problems.socraticHint: Which part of a law tells you where somebody is, and which part tells you how fast they are getting somewhere?

variant.prompt: Suppose Ana's distance is d = 50t + 300 and Ben's is d = 50t + 120. Which sentence is true?
options: They walk at the same pace and Ana starts ahead
They start level and Ana pulls away

problems.prompt: Ana's distance is d = 70t + 200 and Ben's is d = 90t. After how many minutes is Ben level with Ana?
explanation: Level means both laws give the same distance, so set them equal: 90 times t equals 70 times t plus 200.
Take 70 times t off both pans, leaving 20 times t equal to 200.
Share both pans by 20, and t is 10 minutes.
Check it back in: both walkers are 900 m from the gate.
problems.useAgain: when two steady things are chasing each other and you want the moment they are equal.
hints: Level is a sentence about distances, not about who is faster. Write that sentence as one equation.
The letter is sitting in both pans. Take the smaller pile of it off both sides first.
problems.socraticHint: Before that moment, who is in front, and does the answer to that ever change again afterwards?

variant.prompt: Ana's distance is d = 60t + 240 and Ben's is d = 100t. After how many minutes is Ben level with Ana?

problems.prompt: Suppose the tin started the day with a float and every bracelet sold adds the same amount to it. The tally read 16 dollars after 2 bracelets, 34 dollars after 5, and 58 dollars after 9. True or false: those three readings sit on one straight line.
explanation: A straight line means the same per all along, so test the per across each gap.
From 2 bracelets to 5, the tin gained 18 dollars across 3 bracelets: 6 dollars a bracelet.
From 5 to 9, it gained 24 dollars across 4 bracelets: 6 dollars a bracelet again.
The per never changed, so the readings do sit on one line.
problems.useAgain: when a table of readings might or might not be a line, and you need to decide which before trusting it.
hints: Do not look at the totals. Look at what changed between one reading and the next.
Work out the dollars per bracelet for each gap, then compare the gaps with each other.
problems.socraticHint: If one gap gave a different per from another, could a single straight line still pass through all three readings?

variant.prompt: Suppose the tally read 20 dollars after 3 bracelets, 38 dollars after 6, and 60 dollars after 10. True or false: those readings sit on one straight line.

problems.prompt: Using that same tally, 16 dollars after 2 bracelets, 34 after 5 and 58 after 9, what will the tin hold after 12 bracelets?
explanation: The per is 6 dollars a bracelet, from 18 dollars gained across 3 bracelets.
Wind one reading back to no bracelets at all: 16 dollars minus two lots of 6 leaves a float of 4 dollars.
So the law of this line is 6 times the count of bracelets, plus 4.
Twelve bracelets bring 72 dollars, and the float was already there, so the tin holds 76 dollars.
problems.useAgain: when a table gives you a line and you need a reading it never actually took.
hints: Find the dollars per bracelet first, then find what was in the tin before a single one sold.
Wind one of the readings back to zero bracelets by taking off that many pers.
problems.socraticHint: Which part of the law would change if the float had been bigger, and which part would not move at all?

variant.prompt: Suppose the tally read 21 dollars after 3 bracelets and 45 dollars after 9. What will the tin hold after 15 bracelets?

steps.title: The point exactly between two others, and choosing without an order

problems.prompt: A segment runs from (2, 3) to (8, 7). What are the coordinates of its midpoint?
explanation: A midpoint is just the average of the two x's and the average of the two y's.
Average the x's: 2 plus 8 is 10, divided by 2 is 5.
Average the y's: 3 plus 7 is 10, divided by 2 is 5.
The midpoint is (5, 5).
problems.useAgain: when the exact middle point of a segment is needed, by averaging the x's and averaging the y's separately.
hints: Average the two x-coordinates by themselves first.
Then average the two y-coordinates by themselves.
problems.socraticHint: Does the midpoint's x-coordinate depend on either endpoint's y-coordinate at all?

variant.prompt: A segment runs from (1, 4) to (5, 10). What are the coordinates of its midpoint?

problems.prompt: A segment runs from (-3, 5) to (7, -1). What are the coordinates of its midpoint?
explanation: Average the x's: -3 plus 7 is 4, divided by 2 is 2.
Average the y's: 5 plus -1 is 4, divided by 2 is 2.
The midpoint is (2, 2), even though one endpoint sits in negative territory.
problems.useAgain: when one or both endpoints have negative coordinates, since averaging still works exactly the same way.
hints: Adding a negative number is the same as subtracting; average the x's carefully first.
Then do the same for the y's.
problems.socraticHint: Does a negative coordinate change how you average two numbers, or just what the sum comes out to?

variant.prompt: A segment runs from (-6, -2) to (2, 8). What are the coordinates of its midpoint?

problems.prompt: A pizza shop offers 4 toppings: pepperoni, mushroom, onion, olive. How many different 2-topping combinations can you choose, where order does not matter?
explanation: Choosing pepperoni-and-mushroom is the same combination as mushroom-and-pepperoni, so order does not create a new one.
Listing every pair without repeats gives 6: there is no faster shortcut needed yet at this size.
This kind of count, choosing a group where order does not matter, is called a combination.
problems.useAgain: when a group is being chosen and the order the members are picked in does not matter.
hints: Try listing every possible pair of toppings without repeating a pair in reverse order.
Pepperoni-mushroom and mushroom-pepperoni are the same combination, not two.
problems.socraticHint: If picking topping A then topping B gives the same pizza as picking B then A, should both orders be counted separately?

variant.prompt: A pizza shop offers 5 toppings. How many different 2-topping combinations can you choose, where order does not matter?

problems.prompt: A shop offers 6 flavors of ice cream. How many different 2-scoop combinations can you make using two different flavors, where order does not matter?
explanation: Vanilla-then-chocolate and chocolate-then-vanilla are the same 2-scoop combination.
Counting every different pair of flavors without double-counting the reverse order gives 15.
The bigger the flavor list gets, the faster this count grows.
problems.useAgain: when choosing 2 different items from a larger set, and the order they were picked in does not matter.
hints: Would swapping the order of the two scoops make a different combination?
Count every different unordered pair from the 6 flavors.
problems.socraticHint: Does a 2-scoop cup taste different depending on which scoop you put in first?

variant.prompt: A shop offers 7 flavors of ice cream. How many different 2-scoop combinations can you make using two different flavors, where order does not matter?

steps.title: The bridges, and the drawings that can be walked

problems.prompt: Chalk Konigsberg on the driveway: four pieces of land and seven bridges. The island joins the north bank by 2 bridges, the south bank by 2 bridges, and the east land by 1. The east land joins the north bank by 1 bridge and the south bank by 1. Count the bridges touching each piece of land. How many pieces of land have an odd number?
explanation: Take one piece of land at a time and count every bridge that touches it.
The island has 5. The east land has 3. The north bank has 3. The south bank has 3.
Every one of those counts is odd.
Then walk it with your feet before you believe any arithmetic about it. Nobody in the town ever managed all seven bridges without repeating one.
problems.useAgain: when a map of places and links is really a drawing of dots and lines, and you want to know what meets where.
hints: Take one piece of land at a time and count the bridge ends touching it, not the bridges on the whole map.
Write the count beside each piece of land in chalk, then look at which counts are odd.
problems.socraticHint: If you counted every bridge end on the whole map, how many times would each single bridge get counted?

variant.prompt: Suppose the town builds one more bridge, joining the north bank straight to the south bank. Now how many pieces of land have an odd number of bridges?

problems.prompt: Chalk each of these and try it for real. Which one can you not draw without lifting the chalk and without going over any line twice?
options: a square with one diagonal drawn
a square with both diagonals drawn, crossing in the middle
a figure eight, two circles touching at a single point
explanation: Try all four with real chalk first. Three of them come out, though one only from the right starting corner.
The triangle and the figure eight close up on themselves. The square with one diagonal works if you start at a corner that diagonal reaches.
The square with both diagonals strands you every time, from every corner and from the crossing too.
Now count the lines meeting each corner on all four, and write those counts down. Something about the odd ones is worth staring at.
problems.useAgain: when a puzzle is about tracing or walking, and turning the picture into corners and lines is the first honest move.
hints: Chalk is cheap. Try each one from several different starting points before you rule anything out.
When one of them strands you, count how many lines meet at each corner of that drawing.
problems.socraticHint: In the drawings that did work, did it matter where you started?

variant.prompt: Which one of these can you draw without lifting the chalk and without going over any line twice?
options: a square with both diagonals drawn
the Konigsberg map, four lands and seven bridges
a square with a smaller square inside it and all four matching corners joined
two triangles side by side sharing one whole side

problems.prompt: Five camps are chalked on the drive. Tracks run A to B, A to C, A to D, B to C, C to E and D to E. How many camps have an odd number of tracks?
explanation: Every track has two ends, and each end adds one to the count at the camp it lands on.
A touches three tracks, B touches two, C touches three, D touches two and E touches two.
Only A and C came out odd.
problems.useAgain: when a list of links is handed to you in words and you need the count at each place before anything else.
hints: Go camp by camp, not track by track, or you will count some tracks twice over and miss others entirely.
Write the six tracks out as a list and tick each camp off as you meet it.
problems.socraticHint: Add up all five counts. Is that total odd or even, and could it ever have come out odd?

variant.prompt: Tracks run A to B, A to C, A to D, A to E, B to C and D to E. How many camps have an odd number of tracks?

problems.prompt: Chalk all four of these and count the corners that have an odd number of lines meeting there. Put them in order, fewest odd corners first.
items: a square with both diagonals drawn
a hexagon with the three diagonals that pass through its middle drawn
a square with one diagonal drawn
explanation: The triangle has two lines at each of its three corners, so nothing there is odd.
The square with one diagonal has three lines at two corners and two at the others.
The square with both diagonals has three at every corner, and four where they cross.
The hexagon has three at each of its six corners, and six at the crossing.
problems.useAgain: when several drawings need comparing and the only fair comparison is the same count taken on every one.
hints: The crossing point in the middle of a drawing is a corner too, and lines meet there.
Count the lines at every corner of one drawing and total the odd ones before moving to the next drawing.
problems.socraticHint: Which of these four did you manage in one stroke, and where do those ones sit in your order?

variant.prompt: Same job, three drawings this time. Order them, fewest odd corners first.
items: two circles touching at a single point
the Konigsberg map, four lands and seven bridges
a square with one diagonal drawn

problems.prompt: Go back to the five camps, the map with exactly two odd camps. Try to walk every track exactly once, starting from each of the five camps in turn. What happens?
options: it works only when you start at one of the two odd camps
it works only when you start at a camp with an even number of tracks
explanation: Five camps means five quick experiments. Starting at A you can finish, and starting at C you can finish.
One route from A: A to B, B to C, C to E, E to D, D to A, A to C. It ends at C.
Starting at B, D or E you always run out with a track unwalked.
You found that by trying, which is the right way round this week. Proving it is next week's job.
problems.useAgain: when experiments are cheap and you would rather collect the evidence yourself than be handed a rule.
hints: Five starting camps, so five experiments. Do all of them before you answer.
When a walk fails, notice which camp you were standing on when the tracks ran out.
problems.socraticHint: When a walk did work, where did it finish?

variant.prompt: Now the triangle, which has no odd corners at all. Try walking every line exactly once, starting from each corner in turn. What happens?
options: it works only from one particular corner
it works from every corner, and each time you finish where you started
it works from exactly two of the corners

problems.prompt: A peak in the AMC 8 style, untimed, and you explain it back afterwards. A candle burns down at a steady rate. After 12 minutes it stands 21 cm tall, and after 30 minutes it stands 15 cm tall. How tall was it at the moment it was lit?
explanation: Between the two readings, 18 minutes passed and the candle lost 6 cm.
So it loses 6 cm every 18 minutes, which is a third of a centimetre each minute.
Wind back from the earlier reading: 12 minutes before it, the candle was 12 thirds taller, which is 4 cm.
So it stood 21 plus 4 cm at lighting. Steady burning is a line in disguise, with a negative slope.
problems.useAgain: when something changes steadily and you are asked about a moment before or after the readings you were given.
hints: This is a line wearing a costume. Find how much it changes each minute before anything else.
Wind the earlier reading backwards to the moment of lighting, using that per.
problems.socraticHint: Which of the two readings is nearer the moment it was lit, and which way does the height go as you travel back?

variant.prompt: Same candle, different readings: after 10 minutes it stands 18 cm and after 25 minutes it stands 12 cm. How tall was it when it was lit?

problems.prompt: A peak in the AMC 8 style, untimed, and you explain it back afterwards. Seven dots are drawn and some pairs are joined by lines. True or false: three of the dots could have exactly one line each while the other four have exactly three lines each.
explanation: Add up the line counts at every dot: three dots with one line is 3, four dots with three lines is 12, so 15 altogether.
Every line has two ends, and each end adds one to the count at one dot.
So that total is always twice the number of lines, and twice anything is even.
15 is odd, so no such drawing exists at all, however long you sit there trying to draw one.
problems.useAgain: when someone claims a drawing or a set of links exists and you want to rule it out without drawing anything.
hints: Add up all seven of the counts before you try drawing a single line.
Ask what that total is actually counting. Not dots, and not quite lines either.
problems.socraticHint: If you snipped every line in half, how many loose ends would be lying on the floor?

variant.prompt: True or false: three of the seven dots could have exactly two lines each while the other four have exactly three lines each.

steps.title: The month 1 monster opens: Josephus
steps.body:
This one is not for today. It is for the month.

Ten coins in a circle, numbered 1 to 10. Start at coin 1, leave it, and take coin 2 away. Keep going round, always leaving one and taking the next, until a single coin is left. Which number survives?

Do it with real coins on the floor, not in your head. Then do the same for a circle of 4 coins, then 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9, and write the survivor beside each size in the field journal.

That table is the whole job for now. Nothing is due today, nothing is due this week, and there is nothing to type into the app about it. Add a circle whenever you feel like one, and keep every answer on one page where you can see them all at once, because they only start talking to each other when they are side by side.

Two rules. Act every circle out with your hands, because the ones you only imagine come out wrong. And do not look it up. A month of your own guessing is worth more than one afternoon of somebody else's answer, and at the week 4 summit that table is yours to bring and yours to explain.

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Write the law of your own line into the field journal. Take the tin tally from the skills lane, or the dawn walk if you would rather use your own feet, and write three things: the per and what it is a per of, the starting amount and what it means in the real thing, and then the whole law on one line. Finish with a sentence a stranger could read without any of this in front of them: what does the slope actually mean here, said in bracelets or metres and not in letters.

steps.title: Explain back
steps.prompt: Chalk Konigsberg on the driveway, four lands and seven bridges, and hand it to a grown-up: walk every bridge exactly once, no repeats, take your time. Let them try properly, twice. Then record yourself: the counts you wrote beside each piece of land, what happened when they tried, and what you now suspect decides whether a drawing can be walked in one go. Say suspect and not know, because you have not proved a thing yet.

extras.title: How your brain keeps this
extras.body:
Before the season starts, ten minutes on how your own brain keeps things. Everything in this app is built on it.

1. Reading something again feels like learning. It mostly is not. Pulling it back out of your head, without looking, is what makes it stay. That is why the mistake box brings a problem back weeks later in a new shape.
2. The gap matters. A thing you meet in week 3 and again in week 7 sticks far better than a thing you meet twice in one afternoon. The warm-ups do this on purpose.
3. Sleep is when the day's learning gets filed. A hard bar practised before bed is easier in the morning for a reason.
4. A mistake is data, not a mark against you. Finding out you were sure and wrong is the most useful moment of the week. That is why the app asks what made it feel certain.
5. Small and often beats long and rare. Four sittings of fifteen minutes teach more than one hour, in music and in math alike.
